newsitem.title: GERMANY: NATO to admit new members, and regret it -- Lebed.
newsitem.headline: NATO to admit new members, and regret it -- Lebed.

text.p: Russian presidential hopeful Alexander Lebed said on Tuesday he expected NATO to admit four new members despite Moscow's objections but believed further alliance expansion would falter.
Moscow has recently made a number of hard-line statements expressing its opposition to NATO recruiting new members among former Soviet satellite states in eastern Europe.
The first wave of new members, widely expected to be Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic and possibly Slovenia, are due to be named in July.

"I am convinced NATO will admit these four countries. Then internal tensions will grow so much within the bloc they will be the last countries to be admitted to NATO," Lebed, beginning a five-day visit to Germany, told ARD national television.

Lebed, who was briefly made President Boris Yeltsin's security adviser after coming third in a presidential election last June, said this did not mean he accepted NATO expansion, and stressed the need to talk to NATO.
The Western alliance hopes such a dialogue will give Russia a firm place in Europe's security architecture and reassure it that NATO expansion is not a threat to its security.
"We don't want Russia to be weakened and we must sort that out in the course of our work," he said.

"We have to establish a clear goal. If we want to build up a security zone, then any security system, whether European or global, is pointless without Russia. Russia is a part of Europe, we really do have to do this together."

The 46-year-old retired general appeared to disagree with the approach of Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, who last month surprised his NATO counterparts by rejecting an offer to exchange military liaison officers.
"We should raise the level of mutual trust, take responsibilty. For that we need Russian representation at NATO, so that we can work together on these questions of peace, and not as rivals."
Lebed has several times called for Yeltsin to step down because of his ill health. He has made clear he wants to become president.
His visit has the clear aim of introducing him to the political and economic establishment in Germany, where Chancellor Helmut Kohl is one of Yeltsin's staunchest supporters.
He is being received by top representatives of all the parliamentary parties as well as leading industrialists.
Lebed said he had 80 percent support among the Russian population, and that he could end the chaos now besetting the country.
"Perhaps I'm being immodest but I can cite the fact that I have ended two wars (in Moldova and Chechnya)," he said.
"I can do this, I can bring order, civilised order, introduce a 'dictatorship of law'...We have very favourable conditions for that." REUTER
